## Why This Is Asked
Diagnoses disk pressure across diverse filesystems in real deployments. Requires precise parsing of df outputs, handling spaces, and edge cases like pseudo filesystems. A pragmatic check supports reliability in production.

## Key Concepts
- df usage and -P portability
- inode vs block usage metrics
- robust parsing with awk/shell while handling spaces
- filtering pseudo filesystems

## Code Example
```bash
# robust per-mount health check (blocks and inodes)
df -P | awk 'NR>1{mount=$NF; blocks[switch(mount)]=substr($5,1,length($5)-1); mounts[mount]=1} END{for (m in blocks) print m":"" blocks="blocks[m]"%""," inodes="inodes[m]"%"" - ok"}'
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to reason about log-stability and data integrity across plain and JSON formats, including gzipped rotated files, using only standard tools.

## Key Concepts
- Looping over multiple service dirs
- Handling plain text and JSON lines
- Decompressing gzip with gzip -t and zcat
- tail -c to inspect last byte
- POSIX shell compatibility considerations

## Code Example
```javascript
for d in /logs/service-*/; do
  s=${d##*/}; s=${s%%/*}; p=0
  for f in "$d"/*.log "$d"/*.log.gz; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    if gzip -t "$f" 2>/dev/null; then c=$(zcat "$f" | tail -c 1); else c=$(tail -c 1 "$f"); fi
    if [ -n "$c" ] && [ "$c" != $'\\n' ]; then p=1; break; fi
  done
  [ "$p" -eq 1 ] && echo "$s:PARTIAL" || echo "$s:CLEAN"
done | sort
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt to multiple active symlinks per service?
- How would you validate this in a CI with synthetic partial-lines?

- Reboot as last resort if process won't recover
